name: Naman
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Crowley, Terry (ed. John Lynch). 2006. Naman: A vanishing language of Malakula (Vanuatu). Pacific Linguistics 576. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, RSPAS, Australian National University. xxii+287 pp. DOI 10.15144/PL-576; hdl 1885/146276 (ANU Open Research, open access, CC BY-SA 4.0).
catalog_locator: Crowley 2006, ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.1.4 'Stress', pp. 39-40; phonotactics of vowel sequences sec. 2.2 p. 41.
catalog_quote: [Crowley 2006:39] Stress is assigned to the penultimate syllable in Naman unless the final syllable contains two vowels, in which case it is that syllable which receives stress. When the final syllable contains a long vowel, that vowel also receives stress. Thus: /neni/ ['neni] 'coconut' /noutiret/ [nou'tiret] 'perspiration' /nereun/ [ne'reun] 'leaf' /nuvuoi/ [nuvu'oi] 'roof beam' /delva:t/ [ndel'va:t] 'at midnight' ... Syllables containing schwa are treated in the same way as any other vowels for the purposes of stress assignment. This means that schwas can also be stressed ... Stress is not fixed to a particular syllable of a root in Naman. Thus, when a root receives a suffix that is at least one syllable in length, stress shifts predictably to the right according to the generalisations just presented. Thus: /bə-mən/ ['mbəmən] 'I will drink it' /bə-sə-mən-si/ [mbəsə'mənsi] 'I will not drink it' ... those schwas which are eligible for optional deletion under the conditions set out in §2.1.2.2 are ignored for syllable-counting purposes in stress assignment. Thus, stress is applied to the final syllable of a word when the penultimate syllable contains deletable schwa, as in the following: /gəlo/ [gə'lo] '(s)he looked'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; it falls on the final syllable instead when that syllable contains a vowel sequence (diphthong) or a long vowel. Schwa syllables count and may bear stress, but schwas eligible for optional deletion (sec. 2.1.2.2) are invisible to the syllable count, so stress can surface as final (e.g. /gəlo/ [gə'lo]) or land on a preceding full-syllable prefix. Syllabic nasals and liquids count as syllable nuclei (so /nəvern/ with syllabic final n is stressed [nə'vern]). Stress is computed over the whole inflected word and shifts rightward when syllabic suffixes are added.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in 2.1.4.
new_statements.exceptions: Final stress when the final syllable has two vowels or a long vowel; optionally deletable schwas skipped in syllable counting (yielding surface-final stress or stress on a full-syllable prefix); syllabic liquids/nasals treated as vowels for counting. Elsewhere (e.g. sec. on compounds/serial verbs, p. ~ lines citing 2.1.4) some tightly bound sequences are stressed as a single phonological word while others keep separate word stresses.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (inflected) phonological word including prefixes and suffixes; examples are citation forms of nouns and inflected verbs. Rule is right-edge, quantity-conditioned only at the final syllable (VV or V: final attracts stress), otherwise fixed penultimate.
new_statements.identity_note: Crowley 2006 describes Naman (also known by the village name Litzlitz, whence the glottocode litz1237; ISO 639-3 lzl), central-northwest Malakula, Vanuatu, based on the last fluent speakers; no dialect split is relevant to the stress statement. Note: the PDF text encodes schwa as a private-use glyph (U+F0AB), so schwas are missing from the extracted text output; the quoted rule sentences are unaffected.
